newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan opposition leader sees LDP drifting to right.
newsitem.headline: Japan opposition leader sees LDP drifting to right.

text.p: The loose parliamentary alliance between Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party and two smaller parties is showing signs of strain, an opposition leader said on Friday.
"I think you're going to see a change in the relationship between the LDP and its partners in government," Democratic Party leader Nato Kan told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.
"And I think that means you will see this government turn slightly more conservative."
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's LDP lacks a majority in parliament but has worked with a loose alliance including the left-leaning Social Democratic Party and the Sakigake party.

Members of both of those parties have expressed reluctance to back Hashimoto's efforts to push legislation through parliament allowing U.S. bases to continue occupying land on the southern island of Okinawa despite opposition from local landowners.
But on Thursday, Hashimoto struck a deal with the largest opposition party, Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), ensuring smooth passage of the controversial bill.
Hashimoto said passage of the bill was needed to meet a May 14 deadline on expiry of leases on private land for U.S. military facilities on Okinawa.
Kan said Hashimoto's deal with Shinshinto leader Ichiro Ozawa shows the LDP is moving toward a more conservative-oriented alliance with that party.

"If this conservative-conservative coalition develops, we will look to develop a counter-balancing liberal-reform group," Kan said, adding that such a grouping could also include Sakigake and Taiyo (Sun), a Shinshinto splinter group led by ex-premier Tsutomu Hata.

A larger grouping to take in the Social Democratic Party depends on whether that party fully renounces its former opposition to maintaining U.S. armed forces in Japan and the security treaty with the United States, Kan said.

The Democratic Party could still decide to back the government-sponsored bill on U.S. military bases next week if the LDP pledges to re-negotiate force levels and deployment with the United States, Kan said.
The Democratic Party supports a U.S. naval and air force presence in Japan, but says that the Marines based in Okinawa could be relocated to Hawaii or Guam.
The Democrats hold 52 seats in the 500-seat Lower House and 15 seats in the 252-seat Upper House, making it the second-largest opposition party after Shinshinto.
